name: The Errand
description: Four optional checks around a simple collection run into the city. None of them gate the scene and none of them cost anything on a failure -- same zero-stakes rule as The Road In and Kit Issue. The scene's actual content is the conversation with the old man, and that is reached by talking to him, never by passing a check.

checks.name: Find somebody who can read the docket

dc.basis: level 1 DC 15, no adjustment -- offered to the whole table, not a specialist's roll

outcomes.criticalSuccess: Third person they ask points straight across the street -- and says it warmly: "Old fella in the tea house. He used to be something, I think. Nice to whoever's nice to him." That warmth is real width: whichever PC gets it can open the actual conversation already halfway trusted, not from a cold start.
outcomes.success: A few wrong turns, then somebody mentions the tea house.
outcomes.failure: Nobody in the quarter knows, and several are cheerfully certain the docket is a misprint. They find him anyway -- he is sitting where he always sits, and he has been watching six lost trainees for ten minutes with open interest.
outcomes.criticalFailure: As failure, and one of the people they asked will remember six Directorate trainees asking odd questions. Nothing comes of it tonight.

checks.name: Take a proper look at him

dc.basis: level 1 DC 15, one step hard -- most of the table won't get this, and that's the point

outcomes.criticalSuccess: Everything below, and the thing that matters: he notices being looked at, and he is not used to it. Whatever else happens in this scene, he has decided he likes this one.
outcomes.success: A chemist, and not a recent one. Old stains at the first and second fingers that no longer wash out. He reads the docket the way a musician reads music -- he is not working it out, he is hearing it. Poor, and careful about not looking it. His coat has been mended well, by hand, more than once.
outcomes.failure: An old man in a tea house. Nothing else.
outcomes.criticalFailure: An old man in a tea house, and a faint conviction that he is nobody at all. Do not correct it.

bySkill.perception: The physical read: stains at the first and second fingers, old enough they've stopped trying to scrub out. A coat mended by hand, more than once, by someone who cared how the stitches sat, not just that they held.
bySkill.medicine: The stains aren't just old -- they're a specific old, the kind that comes from years of a trade that's since gone rough on him. A faint, controlled tremor in the reading hand, the kind a body learns to manage rather than the kind that's new. Whatever he did with those hands, he did it for a long time, and stopped a while ago.
bySkill.society: Poor, in the specific way that takes real effort to keep looking like dignity instead. The coat isn't just mended, it's mended to a standard he clearly still holds himself to -- someone who used to matter to people, and has arranged his whole presentation so nobody currently has to know that.

dc.basis: level 1 DC 15, one step hard -- matches a-mark-at-head-height in c1e1-the-road-in exactly, on purpose

outcomes.criticalSuccess: Same deep violet, same neat hand, same height. And this one is on the wall people face while they queue for the store -- not on the road side, where it would be seen by traffic. It is placed for standing crowds.
outcomes.success: The same mark they may have seen on the way in. Same colour, same height. Somebody has been doing this for a while.

bySkill.occultism: The stroke order is deliberate, not decorative -- drawn the way a working mark gets drawn, in one unbroken motion, not the way a tag or a signature gets drawn. Whoever does this isn't just leaving a symbol. They're placing something.
bySkill.crafting: Marine primer again, and the same batch by the colour: whoever is doing this buys it by the tin from a ships' chandler, not from a hardware shop, and there are only so many chandlers in a harbour town.
bySkill.society: It's exactly the kind of thing that should have been painted over by now -- a wall like this gets noticed, complained about, scrubbed. It hasn't been. Somebody either owns that wall's silence, or nobody with the authority to mind has looked at it twice.

checks.name: Get anything at all out of the storekeeper

dc.basis: level 1 DC 15, one step easy -- this is a treat, not a test

outcomes.criticalSuccess: She finds the item in under a minute once she knows what it actually is, throws in something small she can't sell, and tells them which of the three chandlers on this stretch waters their primer.
outcomes.success: Cheerful, unhurried, and completely unable to help until somebody tells her what the docket means.
outcomes.failure: She has a queue, they are six teenagers in brand-new uniforms, and the docket is somebody else's problem.
outcomes.criticalFailure: As failure, and she calls them 'the Directorate' for the rest of the scene, in the tone you'd use for a utility company.

bySkill.diplomacy: She warms to them specifically -- kindness answered with kindness. If anyone asks her something later in the scene, she remembers being asked nicely now.
bySkill.deception: Nineteen years behind this counter means she has heard every version of 'we definitely know what we're doing' there is, and isn't fooled for a second -- it costs nothing, but SHE gets to be the one who's in on the joke, not just the one explaining it.
bySkill.intimidation: It works about as well as intimidating someone with nineteen years and a queue behind them ever does -- she gets flatter, not more helpful. Play it as comic deflation, never a real cost; the DC and the outcome table are identical to any other skill here.
bySkill.society: She clocks that they actually understand how a stores request is supposed to work, and treats them as competent rather than lost -- a small, real difference in how much she volunteers without being asked.

notes:
NONE OF THESE REACH MANAKO, DELIBERATELY. The docket's obsolete catalogue name is not decodable by a level-1 character at any DC -- it is a dead naming convention, not a hard knowledge check, so there is no roll that lets the party skip the old man. read-the-old-man is the only check that touches him at all, and what it buys is warmth, not information.

The contact route he offers at the end of the scene is NOT gated on a check either. It is earned by talking to him like a person. A table that rolls badly and is kind still gets it; a table that rolls well and treats him as a vending machine does not. That is the whole design of the scene and it should not be turned into a skill gate.

HOW FAR CAN A GREAT ROLL GO HERE. A natural 20 on a social check needs an answer ready before it happens, and for this scene the answer is that these four checks are deliberately capped at warmth, speed and texture, never information about Manako himself or the campaign's larger mysteries -- that is a design choice rather than caution by omission, because the scene's real width-of-action lever is the choicePoint at the-vial's follow-up beat (how they file the requisition) and the split-party search structure, not crit-success revelation. A genuinely new approach that is not one of these four should still be priced on the standard ladder (13/15/17/20) per this project's usual rule -- it just won't unlock Manako's identity or anything past what read-the-old-man already caps at, because nothing in this scene is built to give that up yet.
